persona_name: Condensed-matter physicist and systems-performance skeptic: memory device reliability, DRAM bandwidth/latency physics, die aging and long-term storage; reviews for IEDM/ISCA-adjacent venues

objections.section: §0 POSSIBLE (17 tok/s, 4 concurrent, ~27 users) / §1 'The CPU reads only the picked experts' / §2.3 L and S rows / INPUTS L_single_tps, S_single_tps / capacity()
objections.objection: Both SKUs' user counts sit on rounding knife-edges, and the L input is scaled by parameters the CPU never reads. (1) Knife-edge. capacity() counts c users only if single x min(c^0.62, 2.4)/c >= 10 tok/s. For the L box that needs a single stream of >=16.93 tok/s for 4 users, >=15.18 for 3 and >=13.01 for 2 (my run of the model's own functions). L_single_tps = 17.0 clears 4 users by 0.4% (10.04 tok/s each). At 16.9 the L box serves 3 users, 20 named users, $155 per user per month. S_single_tps = 25.0 sits exactly on the c = 6 line (25 x 2.4/6 = 10.00). Its measured basis, 32.1/1.29 = 24.88, gives 5 users, 33 named users and $48 instead of 6, 40 and $40. (2) Wrong bytes. The input scales R1's 8.73 tok/s by '37/32 active params' (+16%). But the CPU holds only the routed experts, and those are almost the same size in both models. DeepSeek-R1 routes 8 experts of 3x7168x2048 = 44.0M params over 58 MoE layers: 20.4B params. Kimi-K2.x routes 8 over 60 MoE layers: 21.1B. Kimi's smaller active count comes from 64 attention heads instead of 128 and 1 dense layer instead of 3, all GPU-resident (public configs) [ESTIMATE: config arithmetic]. At ~4.5 bits (Kimi INT4, group 32) against ~4.5-4.8 bits (R1 Q4_K_M), the right factor is ~0.97-1.03, not 1.156. 8.73 x 2.0 x 1.03 x 0.85 = 15.3 tok/s, which gives 3 users and 20 named users. With the 6,000 MT/s platform limit in RT-VET-DD6-01 (x1.875) it is 14.3 tok/s: 2 users, 13 named users. (3) Wrong cross-check. The input says MiniMax-M2.1 reads '~0.8x Kimi bytes/token'. MiniMax-M2 routes 8 of 256 experts of 3x3072x1536 params over 62 layers: 7.0B params at FP8 = 7.0 GB. Kimi routes 21.1B params at 4.5 bits = 11.9 GB. The ratio is 0.59, not 0.8. So the cross-check gives 24.9 x 0.59 = 14.7 tok/s: 2 users, 13 named users, $232. No public single-socket EPYC 9005 measurement of any 1T MoE exists. The Level1Techs 'Kimi on Epyc' thread has only guesses of 10-20 tok/s (search 2026-11-01). Three independent corrections all land at 13-20 named users, not 27. The model never reads capacity() (RT-VET-DD6-01), so §2.4 does not move.
objections.would_change_my_mind: A Track B single-socket run of Kimi-K2.5 INT4 on the exact BOM (EPYC 9455-class, 12 x 64 GB at the logged MT/s, RTX PRO 6000) measuring >=17.5 tok/s single-stream and >=10 tok/s per user at 4 concurrent with 8k contexts. Or L_single_tps re-derived on routed-expert bytes, the cross-check corrected to 0.59, and §2.3 re-run with capacity() at the corrected values.

objections.section: §1 'One socket, not two' / notes §2.2 ('Dual-socket is poor value') / INPUTS S_single_tps (÷1.29), L_single_tps cross-check / §10 Track B step 1 (rented host)
objections.objection: The 1.29x dual-socket factor is stale, and the deep dive uses it in both directions. It comes from KTransformers v0.2 (Feb-2025), a build that copied every weight onto each NUMA node: 382 GB on one socket against 1 TB on two (notes P1). The engine the deep dive specifies, kt-kernel with SGLang, uses NUMA-aware tensor parallelism. That puts a slice of each expert in each node's local memory, with up to 63% more decode speed on dual-socket systems (LMSYS, 2025-10-22, snippet). (a) Rejecting 2S. With slicing, a 2S board with 24 x 32 GB still holds 768 GB and doubles peak bandwidth. It adds a second $5.5k CPU and ~$1k of board, so ~$8.3k (+13%) on the L box price at 22% GM. At a 1.29-1.63x decode gain, the model's own capacity() gives 5-6 users at >=10 tok/s and 33-40 named users. The 'one socket' design is not supported by current evidence, and the obvious fix for the bandwidth shortfall (RT-VET-DD6-01) is ruled out on a 2025 number. (b) Deriving 1S from the 2S benchmark. P2 (2x EPYC 9355 + RTX 5090, MiniMax-M2.1, 32.1 tok/s) ran on the current NUMA-aware engine. Dividing by 1.29 gives 24.9 tok/s. Dividing by 1.63 gives 19.7 tok/s: 4 users, 27 named users and $60 per user per month for the S box, instead of 6, 40 and $40. The Kimi cross-check then falls to 11.6 tok/s: 1 user, 6.7 named users, $465. (c) Track B. Most rentable 768 GB+ bare-metal hosts are dual-socket [ESTIMATE]. Unless the run is pinned to one socket and its local memory (numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0, with NPS mode and CCD count logged), K4 measures a 2S machine and flatters the 1S SKU by up to 63%.
objections.would_change_my_mind: A current kt-kernel/SGLang run measuring the 1S-to-2S decode gain on the same host (one socket pinned, then both), at or below 1.35x, which would justify the 1S design and the ÷1.29 conversion. Or the L SKU re-specified as 2S with 24 x 32 GB, S_single_tps re-derived with the measured factor, and Track B written to require socket pinning.

objections.section: §1 S SKU ('interactive') / §2.3 S row (40 users, $40/user) / capacity() (no GPU-memory term) / INPUTS S_prefill_*
objections.objection: capacity() has no GPU-memory term, and the S box's 32 GB RTX 5090 runs out of KV cache before it runs out of decode speed. MiniMax-M2 uses grouped-query attention with 8 KV heads x 128 dims over 62 layers: 2 x 62 x 8 x 128 x 2 B = 248 KB per token at BF16, or 124 KB at FP8. The GPU must also hold: ~4.0B non-expert params (attention plus the 200k-vocabulary embeddings), ~4 GB at FP8; a layerwise-prefill double buffer for one layer's 256 experts, 2 x 256 x 14.2M x 1 B = 7.2 GB; ~2 GB of CUDA workspace [ESTIMATE]. That leaves ~19 GB, enough for ~74k tokens of BF16 KV or ~148k at FP8, shared by all users. Six concurrent users at the 32k prompts the S box's own source benchmarks (P2: 2,540 tok/s prefill at 32k) need 192k tokens before any decode, so only 2 users (BF16) to 4 users (FP8) fit. KTransformers' own DeepSeek-V4-Flash doc, for the other S-class model, defaults to MAX_RUNNING_REQUESTS = 2 (notes P8). On RAG-length contexts the S box is a 2-4-user machine. Its $40 per user, the venture's best per-user number, holds only up to ~12k tokens per user. The L box is not affected: its 96 GB card has room for a ~19 GB Kimi layer buffer and MLA KV of ~70 KB per token.
objections.would_change_my_mind: Track B logs peak VRAM and maximum sustained concurrent sessions on the S box at 8k and 32k contexts with FP8 KV, showing >=6 sessions at 32k with no KV eviction or host offload. Or capacity() gets a VRAM/KV constraint and §2.3 is re-run.

objections.section: §0 pitch ('A quiet, U.S.-assembled server') / §3 #7 ('office power and noise bite') / INPUTS L_platform (2 kW PSU), install_h_per_box 8
objections.objection: The L box is a sustained ~1.1-1.3 kW load, not a quiet office appliance, and making it quiet costs memory bandwidth. Power. Nameplate draw [ESTIMATE / UNVERIFIED-training]: EPYC 9455-class at 300 W TDP, RTX PRO 6000 Workstation at 600 W (300 W Max-Q), 12 DDR5 RDIMMs at ~10-13 W each while streaming, plus fans, NVMe and ~92% PSU efficiency. A 120 V/15 A office circuit is limited to 1.44 kW continuous (80% rule). The box leaves no headroom on its circuit and puts ~4,000 BTU/h into whatever closet holds it. Bandwidth. Twelve tightly packed RDIMMs next to a 600 W GPU need server-class airflow to stay below 85 °C. Above 85 °C, DDR5 halves tREFI from 3.9 to 1.95 µs [JESD79-5, UNVERIFIED-training]. With tRFC1 = 295 ns (16Gb die), all-bank refresh then takes 15.1% of device time instead of 7.6%; with 410 ns (24/32Gb die), 21.0% instead of 10.5%. BMC memory throttling acts even earlier. So a 'quiet tower' fan curve taxes exactly the bandwidth the whole capacity case rests on. The model has no line for an electrical survey, a dedicated circuit or cooling, and allows 8 install hours.
objections.would_change_my_mind: A Track B log of wall power, DIMM SPD-hub temperatures and decode tok/s at 4 concurrent users, at a fan curve measured at <=45 dBA at 1 m, showing DIMMs below 85 °C with no throttle events. Plus an install checklist (dedicated 20 A circuit or colo) priced into the setup fee.

objections.section: §1 L SKU (768 GB = 12 x 64 GB, 1 DPC) / §2.2 subscription (3%/yr spare-parts reserve, business-hours SLA) / §11 #13
objections.objection: The L box has no degraded mode for the commonest hardware fault in a large DIMM population. Kimi-K2.5 needs >=600 GB of RAM (>=650 GB per the K2-Thinking native doc, notes P4), and the box has 768 GB in 12 DIMMs. EPYC one-DIMM-per-channel population rules allow balanced sets of 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 or 12 DIMMs per socket [UNVERIFIED-training: AMD memory population guide]. If one DIMM fails, the box has two options: 11 DIMMs, outside the balanced sets, with uneven interleave and lower bandwidth; or 10 DIMMs: 640 GB, below the 650 GB K2-Thinking floor and ~40 GB above K2.5's once OS and staging buffers are counted, with 17% less channel bandwidth (10/12). Since the capacity case is already on a knife-edge (RT-PHY-DD6-01), one failed RDIMM takes the 1T model out of service until an authorized replacement arrives. At BASE m36 the fleet is 22.3 boxes, so ~268 RDIMMs if they were all L boxes. A 0.5-1% per DIMM-year replacement rate [ESTIMATE] gives ~1-3 memory outages a year by m36, and ~8% of DIMMs a year logging correctable errors (Schroeder et al., SIGMETRICS 2009) [UNVERIFIED-training] gives the warning signs. The next-business-day SLA holds only with an on-site spare per L box ($1,898 per 64 GB RDIMM at the model's own price), which the 3%/yr reserve does not hold. This adds to RT-VET-DD6-06, which priced depot spares: the box has no degraded operating point at all.
objections.would_change_my_mind: A Track B test that pulls one RDIMM and shows the L box still serving Kimi-K2.5 INT4 at >=80% of the 12-DIMM decode rate on 11 (or 10) DIMMs. Or the subscription spec and cash model carry one on-site spare RDIMM per L box, plus correctable-error telemetry with a replace threshold.

objections.section: §1 'The MCM' (nine 8Gb x8 die in a 15-20 mm BGA) / §6 FTO #4 ('conventional side-by-side 9-die substrate') / INPUTS mcm_die_per_unit 9, mcm_substrate $60, mcm_assembly $80, good_die_per_wafer (45 mm² basis)
objections.objection: The MCM as described does not fit in its package. The model's own die basis is a 45 mm² DDR4 8Gb die (good_die_per_wafer = 1,251 'at 45 mm², 85% yield'; I reproduce 1,471 gross x 0.85 = 1,251). Nine of them are 405 mm² of bare silicon. That exceeds the whole 20 x 20 mm (400 mm²) envelope and is 135% of a 15 x 20 mm (300 mm²) footprint, before die spacing, bond fingers and the package-edge keep-out. Teledyne's DDR4T04G72, the deep dive's own benchmark, is a 15 x 20 x 1.92 mm, 391-ball, 0.8 mm-pitch multi-chip package, and its datasheet covers both 4 GB and 8 GB in that footprint (Teledyne DS 60S 219460 and Avnet, via search). An 8 GB x72 in 300 mm² therefore needs either 16Gb x16 die (five die, not nine) or die stacking. Stacking center-pad DDR4 die is not a 'conventional side-by-side' substrate. The upper die needs a wafer-level redistribution layer (RDL) to move its center-row pads to the edge, or a face-down window per die, and every die must be thinned to <=~100 µm [ESTIMATE: standard DRAM dual-die-package practice]. RDL is a whole-wafer step on a 300 mm bumping line. It cannot be done on singulated KGD bought from distributor stock (the §10 C4 lot), and on banked wafers it adds a process step. A side-by-side 3 x 3 array needs roughly 29 x 21 mm with spacing and bond fingers [ESTIMATE]. That is a larger part, not pin-compatible, with nine die on one command/address net instead of five for an x16 design: a signal-integrity penalty at DDR4-2400/3200. Cost. The $60 substrate and $80 assembly are side-by-side numbers. At $90 + $160 for a stacked/RDL build [ESTIMATE], my mcm_unit() re-run drops unit GM from 45.6/52.2/61.8% to 32.1/38.8/48.4% (m1/m36/m60), and to 27.3/34.5/44.7% at 85% module yield. §6's 'low risk' FTO reading no longer applies either: stacked-memory packaging (3D Plus, Teledyne, the Irvine Sensors lineage) is a patented field [UNVERIFIED].
objections.would_change_my_mind: A substrate floorplan and quote from a U.S. hi-rel OSAT that shows an 8 GB x72 built from nine 8Gb x8 die in <=15 x 20 mm (or a larger footprint that named target buyers accept in writing). It must state the stacking and RDL steps and cost <=$140 for substrate plus assembly at 300 units/yr, with a die source that supplies whole wafers (for RDL) or pre-RDL'd KGD.

objections.section: §1 'screen it across -55 to 125 °C' / §2.1 L4 row / §5 'Where an entrant could win' #2 / INPUTS mcm_screen $150, mcm_yield 0.91
objections.objection: The -55 to 125 °C claim is a refresh-physics problem, not only a screening-yield problem. JEDEC DDR4 (JESD79-4) defines tREFI = 7.8 µs up to 85 °C and 3.9 µs up to 95 °C Tcase, and nothing above [UNVERIFIED-training]. DRAM cell retention falls roughly exponentially with temperature (Hamamoto et al., IEEE TED 1998; Liu et al., ISCA 2013) [UNVERIFIED-training]. Refresh tax. Extending JEDEC's 2x-per-10 °C convention to 125 °C needs tREFI ≈ 0.49 µs. An 8Gb die's tRFC1 is 350 ns, so the device would spend ~72% of its time refreshing (18% at 105 °C, 36% at 115 °C). Even a gentler Arrhenius fit (Ea 0.5-0.6 eV) puts the 125 °C refresh tax at 23-32% of device time. So a 125 °C x72 part has two options. (a) Derate bandwidth and availability by roughly a quarter to three-quarters when hot, and require the host controller to issue non-JEDEC refresh intervals; many SoC DDR4 controllers stop at 2x [ESTIMATE]. (b) Bin every die for retention at 125 °C. That is a die-level test at temperature, which distributor KGD probed at commercial or industrial temperature has not had. Teledyne sells the same part in two grades, -40 to 105 °C and -55 to 125 °C (search, 2026-11-01), which is what binning looks like. Bin yield enters the module as a ninth power: 98% per die gives 83.4% module yield, 95% gives 63.0%, 90% gives 38.7%. The model has a single 91% yield and one $150 screen, with no temperature-grade split. This adds to RT-VET-DD7-04 (screen fallout) a spec problem that objection does not cover: even a perfect screen does not remove the refresh tax at 125 °C.
objections.would_change_my_mind: Retention-time distributions at 105 and 125 °C on >=100 Winbond or ESMT 8Gb DDR4 die (or a vendor's hot-retention bin data), showing >=98% of die hold data at <=2x JEDEC refresh at 125 °C. Plus an MCM datasheet target that states the 125 °C refresh interval and bandwidth derate, accepted in writing by >=1 NewSpace buyer.

objections.section: §0 POSSIBLE ('Yes (TRL 9)') / §1 'Buy and store' (10-20 years unsawn in nitrogen) / INPUTS pull_yield 0.95 / §11 #11 (>=20% unit-GM buy rule)
objections.objection: The 10-20-year bare-die storage premise rests on evidence about a different object. pull_yield = 0.95 cites Rochester's study of packaged parts that still worked after up to 17 years (DigiKey blog); there, mold compound covers the bond pads. A banked DRAM wafer has exposed aluminium pads. They already carry probe scrub from two or three sort insertions (hot, cold, post-repair) [ESTIMATE: standard DRAM sort flow], and §1's plan adds a re-probe touchdown at pull. The bare-die numbers the deep dive itself cites point the other way. Infineon's own limit for unsawn wafers in nitrogen is 36 months. Micross's '20+ years' is a marketing claim with no published yield. IEC 62435-5 (die and wafer storage) has clauses on bare-die deterioration mechanisms, inert-atmosphere purity, wire bondability and storage time limits, and says compliant storage does not guarantee working parts (VDE and BSI previews, search 2026-11-01). I found no published wire-bond pull or yield data for DRAM die after >=10 years in nitrogen. The physical risks are halogen-residue pad corrosion, a thickened or contaminated aluminium surface, and probe-mark damage that lowers wire-bond pull strength, plus moisture uptake in polyimide overcoats. A 95% electrical pull yield captures none of these bondability risks. Sensitivity (my bank_standalone() re-run, BASE, bought m20): pull yield 0.90 gives unit GM 36.2% and IRR 0.8%; 0.85 gives 32.5%, -1.1% IRR and a 0.95x cash multiple; 0.80 gives 28.3% and -3.2%. Every one of those passes the >=20% unit-GM buy rule (§11 #11), so the rule cannot catch a storage-yield miss. 'TRL 9' holds for Rochester's packaged-part practice and for multi-year wafer storage. For 10-20-year bare DRAM die it is closer to TRL 6-7 [judgment]. The model also carries no surveillance cost: periodic sample assembly and test of each stored lot.
objections.would_change_my_mind: Bond-pull/shear and electrical-yield data on DRAM (or comparable aluminium-pad CMOS) wafers stored >=10 years in nitrogen, for example from Micross or Rochester, showing >=95% assembled yield and bond strength within MIL-STD-883 TM2011 limits. Plus a written vault quote that includes periodic surveillance sampling, carried in the model.

objections.section: §1 'Pull. On an order, re-probe the wafer, saw it, package the die' / INPUTS sell_rate_yr 0.15, pull_units_per_program 80, bank_wafers 10, reprobe/pack/test per unit
objections.objection: 'Pull on demand' cannot be done one order at a time from unsawn wafers, so most banked die spend most of their life in exactly the state the storage case avoids. Thinning, sawing and (for stacks) RDL are whole-wafer steps, so opening a wafer releases ~1,251 die. The model sells 15% a year of 12,510 die (~156 a month in BASE), and an L1 program draws 80 die a month. Each opened wafer therefore sits for ~8 months (L3) to ~16 months (L1) as singulated die on dicing tape, in waffle packs or in gel-paks. Dicing and UV tape adhesion and residue change with age; tape makers typically state shelf life in months, not years [ESTIMATE/UNVERIFIED]. Singulated die also face handling, edge-chipping and contamination risks that unsawn wafers do not. Each alternative has a cost the model leaves out: (a) package the whole wafer when it is opened and store packaged parts, the mode Rochester's 17-year data actually supports. That front-loads ~1,251 x $11.50 = ~$14.4k of pull cost per wafer, plus dry-pack and MSL handling. (b) accept a shorter-life singulated-die inventory. The model books pull cost per unit sold instead. It is also unverified that the small U.S. houses named (QP Technologies, Integra) can backgrind and saw 300 mm DRAM wafers; thinning 300 mm wafers to <=100 µm needs a large-OSAT tool set.
objections.would_change_my_mind: A written vault or OSAT process for partial-wafer pulls, for example sawing and re-sealing the remaining die in nitrogen with a stated shelf life of >=24 months. Or the model changed to package a whole wafer at each opening. Plus a U.S. OSAT quote for 300 mm DRAM backgrind and saw.

objections.section: §10 Track C4 (Suntsu ESMT KGD lot) / §2.7 #1 (OCM list) / INPUTS good_die_per_wafer (45 mm²), mcm_die_per_unit 9, bank_wafers 10
objections.objection: The die the kill test would buy is not the die the model uses, and the model's die is not one the plausible OCM partners make. (1) The Suntsu listing cited in §10 C4 is 'KGD 256Mbx16 DDR4' (URL slug): a 4Gb x16 die. An 8 GB x72 built from 4Gb x16 die needs at least 18 die, and 20 in a practical four-rank build (four data die plus one ECC die per rank), against the MCM's nine. Buying that lot tests the availability of a die the design cannot use, and Track C2's '$400 unit build before die' gate means nothing for it. (2) 1,251 good die per 300 mm wafer assumes a 45 mm² 8Gb die at 85% yield. That is a big-three 1y/1z-class die, from the makers §5 says will not authorize a startup. The OCMs in §2.7 (Winbond, ESMT, Etron, Nanya, Alliance, Intelligent Memory) sell older-node or foundry-made die. At 60-90 mm² [ESTIMATE], a 300 mm wafer yields ~610-930 good die. A 12,510-die bank is then 13.5-20.6 wafers, not 10, and the nine-die MCM silicon is 540-810 mm², which makes RT-PHY-DD7-01 worse. The model prices die per GB, so bank IRR barely moves. Every wafer-count, vault and MCM-area figure in §1, §2.1 and §8 does.
objections.would_change_my_mind: An OCM or distributor quote naming the exact 8Gb x8 DDR4 die that would be banked and used in the MCM (die size, node, gross and good die per wafer). And a §10 C4 purchase of that die instead of the 4Gb x16 lot.

overall.DD6: Buildable, and one user at ~15-17 tok/s is plausible. But both SKUs' user counts sit on knife-edges that the model's own inputs miss: R1-to-Kimi scaling credits parameters the CPU never reads, the MiniMax cross-check uses the wrong byte ratio, and a stale 1.29x socket factor rejects 2S while inflating the S box. Expect ~13-20 named users on L and ~27-33 on S. Measure on a socket-pinned host before quoting anyone.
overall.DD7: The bank's 10-20-year storage premise rests on packaged-part data, and pull-on-demand forces whole-wafer openings. The MCM as drawn does not fit its 15-20 mm package, and at 125 °C it pays a 23-72% refresh tax or needs retention binning that enters yield as a ninth power. No physics rescues the venture case: side line at most, and the MCM line is dead until a stacked, retention-binned design exists.
